inputs.original_text:
More than 58 lakh names have been removed from the electoral roll, and the Supreme Court has ordered tribunals to hear challenges—yet those tribunals are not even operational. That is no way to administer an election. A trustworthy vote depends on accurate rolls and lawful, timely hearings, not bureaucratic drift.

Authorities must get the tribunals working and apply the rules consistently. When basic procedures fail, confidence suffers and political opportunists gain room to stir suspicion. Protecting the integrity of the roll and giving people a fair hearing are both duties of the state.
inputs.modified_text:
More than 58 lakh names have been removed from the electoral roll, and the Supreme Court has ordered tribunals to hear challenges—but those tribunals are still not operational. That is a serious failure of administration. A lawful election requires both accurate rolls and a fair hearing for anyone who believes they were wrongly removed; neither mass suspicion nor automatic reinstatement should replace consistent rules.

The state has a duty to get the tribunals working without delay. When basic procedures break down, public trust erodes and political opportunists are handed an opening to inflame divisions. Electoral integrity depends on orderly administration, equal treatment under the law, and citizens having confidence that the rules are being applied fairly.
